title: Best Tequila for No Hangover: 100% Agave and Additive-Free Picks
excerpt: Which tequila gives you the least hangover? Why 100% agave beats mixto, how to find additive-free tequila, blanco vs reposado, brands people trust, and how to drink it smarter.
metaDescription: Which tequila gives the least hangover? 100% agave vs mixto, additive-free tequila, blanco vs aged, brands to look for, and how to drink it without regret.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** there is no tequila that gives you no hangover. The alcohol itself does most of the damage, so five shots of a beautiful, hand-made blanco will still leave you rough. But tequila is a category where the bottle really does vary a lot, and choosing well can tilt the odds in your favor. The best picks for a gentler morning are **100% agave tequilas, ideally blancos, from producers that don't use additives**. The worst are cheap "mixto" gold tequilas that are only 51% agave and are sweetened and colored to taste smooth.

**The quick rules:** look for **"100% de agave"** on the label. If it doesn't say it, assume it's mixto. Prefer **blanco** over heavily aged or flavored bottles. Check the producer on an **additive-free list** before you buy, because additives don't have to be printed on the label. Then drink it neat, on ice, or with soda water and fresh lime rather than in sugary premixed margaritas. Keep to a modest number of drinks, eat first, and alternate with water.

> **A quick note on safety.** This guide is about choosing tequila and drinking it sensibly. It isn't medical advice. **See a doctor or get emergency care if** someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting repeatedly, has slow or irregular breathing, has cold or bluish skin, or has a seizure. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a bad hangover, so call 911 (in the US) and don't leave them alone to "sleep it off." If you regularly get shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you stop drinking, talk to a doctor, because that can be a sign your body has become dependent on alcohol.

## Why Tequila Has a Bad Reputation (and How Much of It Is Earned)

Ask a room of people about their worst hangover and tequila comes up a lot. Some of that reputation is about the drink and a lot of it is about how people drink it.

**How it gets drunk.** Tequila is the classic shot spirit. Shots go down quickly, usually in rounds, and nobody waits an hour between them. Fast drinking pushes your blood alcohol up faster than your liver can clear it, and the higher your peak, the worse the next morning tends to be. Tequila also gets poured into big, sweet margaritas that are easy to finish in ten minutes.

**What's in the cheap bottles.** For decades, a lot of the tequila sold abroad, especially in bars and at parties, was mixto. That's tequila where only 51% of the sugars come from blue agave and the rest can come from other sources, typically cane sugar. Mixtos are often colored gold with caramel and sweetened to cover harsh flavors. Many people's "tequila hangover" memories are really memories of cheap mixto shots chased with sour mix.

**What the science suggests.** Researchers have long noted that drinks differ in their congeners, the small amounts of other compounds produced during fermentation, distillation, and aging. Congeners give spirits their flavor and color, and some of them, such as methanol and certain fusel alcohols, have been linked to worse hangovers. A well-known study by Rohsenow and colleagues, published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2010, gave volunteers either bourbon or vodka to the same blood alcohol level. Hangovers were somewhat worse after bourbon, the higher-congener drink, although the difference was modest and both groups were hungover. For more on how these compounds work, see our guide to [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol).

There's no good evidence from controlled studies that directly compares different tequilas with each other. So what follows is practical reasoning built on what we do know: how tequila is made, what its rules allow, and how congeners and sugar affect hangovers in general.

## 100% Agave vs Mixto: The Single Most Important Label Check

Real tequila can only be made in Mexico, from one plant: **blue Weber agave** (*Agave tequilana* Weber, blue variety). It has to come from the protected region, which is mainly the state of Jalisco plus some municipalities in Guanajuato, Michoacán, Nayarit, and Tamaulipas. The rules are set by Mexico's official tequila standard and overseen by the Tequila Regulatory Council (the CRT).

Within those rules, there are two kinds of tequila:

| | 100% agave tequila | Mixto tequila |
|---|---|---|
| **Sugar source** | Only blue agave | At least 51% blue agave, up to 49% other sugars (often cane) |
| **Label wording** | "100% de agave" or "100% puro de agave" | Usually just "Tequila," sometimes "gold," "oro," or "especial" |
| **Where it's bottled** | Must be bottled in Mexico | Can be shipped in bulk and bottled elsewhere |
| **Typical price** | Usually $25 and up, with some good bottles under that | Often the cheapest bottles on the shelf |
| **Common additives** | Allowed, but many good producers use none | Very common, especially caramel color in gold mixtos |

**How to tell them apart in five seconds:** look for the words "100% agave." Producers who make 100% agave tequila put it on the label because it's a selling point. If those words aren't there, you're almost certainly holding a mixto.

**Why it may matter for your morning:** mixtos tend to bring along the things most likely to make a night worse. They're often sweetened, which makes them easy to drink fast. They're often colored with caramel to look like aged tequila. And the extra non-agave sugars change the fermentation, which changes the mix of congeners in the finished spirit. None of this has been tested head-to-head in a hangover trial, so it's fair to say the difference is plausible rather than proven. But there's no real downside to buying 100% agave, and it's the one choice almost every tequila expert agrees on.

For a deeper look at tequila-specific hangover science, our article on [the truth about tequila hangovers](/never-hungover/tequila-hangover-truth) walks through it in more detail.

## Additive-Free Tequila: The Check Most People Don't Know About

Here's the part that surprises people. Even a bottle labeled 100% agave can contain additives. Mexican rules allow producers to add small amounts of four types of ingredients without listing them on the label, as long as the total stays under about 1% of the tequila's weight. This practice is called *abocado*, which roughly means "smoothing." The permitted additives are:

- **Caramel color**, to make a tequila look darker or more consistent from batch to batch
- **Oak extract**, to add a barrel-aged flavor without the years in a barrel
- **Glycerin**, to make the tequila feel smoother and thicker in the mouth
- **Sugar-based syrup** (*jarabe*), to add sweetness

One percent sounds tiny, but these ingredients are powerful. A small amount of glycerin and syrup can make a harsh spirit taste soft and sweet. That's the point, and it's also the problem: a tequila that tastes like dessert is a tequila you'll drink faster.

**Is there evidence that additives cause worse hangovers?** Honestly, no. There's no good research on these specific additives at these levels and hangovers. Caramel color and glycerin in these amounts are not known to be harmful. The practical concern is indirect: additives often go with lower-quality base spirit that's been "fixed" to taste better, and they make tequila easier to over-drink. If you want the cleanest, most honest tequila you can buy, additive-free is the way to get it.

**How to find additive-free tequila.** Because additives don't appear on the label, you can't tell by reading the bottle. The most widely used resource is the **Tequila Matchmaker "Confirmed Additive Free" program**, an independent list of brands whose producers have agreed to testing and inspection. It's free to check on their website or app, and it's worth a look before you buy, because the list changes over time as brands are added or removed.

## Blanco, Reposado, Añejo: Does Aging Matter for Hangovers?

Tequila comes in several age classes. Here's what each one means and how it fits into the hangover picture.

| Type | What it is | Hangover angle |
|---|---|---|
| **Blanco (silver, plata)** | Unaged or rested less than two months | Fewest wood-derived congeners. Usually the cleanest choice. |
| **Reposado** | Aged two months to under a year in oak | A bit more from the barrel. Fine if 100% agave and additive-free. |
| **Añejo** | Aged one to three years in small oak barrels | More wood congeners, similar to whiskey territory. Best sipped slowly. |
| **Extra añejo** | Aged more than three years | Richest and most complex. Often expensive, and additives are common in this class. |
| **Joven / oro (gold)** | Usually blanco mixed with aged tequila or colored with caramel | Gold mixtos are the classic hangover bottle. Avoid the cheap ones. |
| **Cristalino** | Aged tequila filtered to remove color | Removes some color compounds, but many cristalinos are sweetened. |

**Why blanco usually wins.** Barrel aging adds flavor compounds from the wood, which is part of why aged spirits are darker. Research on spirits in general, including the bourbon-vs-vodka study above, suggests darker, more congener-rich drinks tend to produce somewhat worse hangovers. A clean blanco sits closer to the vodka end of that scale.

**Why it's not the whole story.** The aging effect is real but modest. A 100% agave, additive-free reposado sipped slowly will usually treat you better than a sweetened mixto blanco taken as fast shots. And añejos are typically sipped, which naturally slows you down. If you love aged tequila, drink it that way rather than switching to blanco and doing rounds.

**A word on cristalinos.** Cristalinos are aged tequilas that have been charcoal-filtered until they're clear. They're marketed as smooth and easy to drink, and many are. Filtering does remove some color compounds, but plenty of cristalinos are also sweetened. "Clear" doesn't automatically mean "clean."

## How It's Made: Ovens, Diffusers, and Why People Argue About It

You'll see tequila fans talk a lot about production methods. Here's a short version so the terms make sense.

To make tequila, the hearts of the agave plant (called *piñas*) are cooked to turn their starches into fermentable sugars. Traditional producers slow-cook them in stone or brick ovens over a day or more, or in pressure cookers called autoclaves. Some large producers use a **diffuser**, a machine that strips sugars out of raw or barely cooked agave with hot water and sometimes chemicals, which is faster and cheaper.

Many tequila experts dislike diffuser-made tequila because they feel it tastes flat or harsh, which is often then covered with additives. That's a flavor and quality argument. There's no good evidence that diffuser-made tequila causes worse hangovers on its own. The connection is the same indirect one: shortcuts in production tend to travel with additives and a sweeter, easier-drinking final product.

If you want a simple rule, you don't need to memorize production methods. Checking "100% agave" on the label and checking the brand against an additive-free list gets you most of the way there.

## What to Look For When You Buy: A Short Checklist

Use this at the store:

1. **"100% de agave" on the label.** Non-negotiable. If it's not there, put it back.
2. **The NOM number.** Every authentic tequila bottle has a NOM number that identifies the distillery that made it. It doesn't tell you about quality on its own, but you can look it up to see who really makes a brand. Many brands are made at the same distillery.
3. **Additive-free status.** Look the brand up on an independent additive-free list before buying. Brands that don't use additives often say so on their website too.
4. **Blanco first.** If you're choosing a tequila mainly for a gentler morning, start with a blanco.
5. **Be wary of "smooth," "gold," "flavored," and dessert-like tasting notes** on cheap bottles. Those are often signs of sweeteners.
6. **Don't use price as your only guide.** Expensive doesn't mean additive-free, and some modestly priced bottles are excellent.

## Brands People Often Recommend (and the Honest Caveats)

We don't sell tequila, and we don't have relationships with any tequila brand. Brand lists go out of date, and a brand's additive-free status can change, so treat this as a starting point and check the current list before you buy.

Brands that have been widely recognized by tequila enthusiasts as 100% agave and **additive-free** at the time of writing include:

- **Fortaleza.** Traditionally made with a stone mill (tahona) and brick ovens. **Pros:** widely respected, clean and agave-forward. **Cons:** can be hard to find and often sells above list price.
- **Siete Leguas.** One of the oldest family producers. **Pros:** traditional methods, consistent. **Cons:** limited distribution in some areas.
- **G4.** **Pros:** known for a bright, very clean blanco. **Cons:** not stocked everywhere.
- **Tequila Ocho.** Known for single-estate releases. **Pros:** interesting for people who want to taste how agave varies by field. **Cons:** batch-to-batch variation is part of the design, which some people don't want.
- **Tapatío.** **Pros:** often a strong value for an additive-free tequila. **Cons:** a robust flavor that some newer drinkers find intense.
- **Cascahuín.** **Pros:** traditional production, well regarded. **Cons:** distribution is spottier than big brands.
- **El Tesoro.** **Pros:** traditionally made and widely available in the US. **Cons:** prices have crept up over time.

A few honest caveats on this list:

- **Being additive-free doesn't make a tequila hangover-proof.** It just means you're getting the spirit without added sweeteners or color. The same number of drinks is still the same amount of alcohol.
- **Big, popular brands aren't automatically bad.** Plenty of well-known 100% agave tequilas are fine choices. If a favorite isn't on an additive-free list, it may use additives or simply may not have gone through the verification process.
- **On a budget, 100% agave is the line that matters most.** Several widely available bottles in the $20 to $30 range are 100% agave. That alone is a big step up from a cheap mixto.

## Tequila vs Other Spirits for a Hangover

Where does tequila sit compared with other drinks? Based on congener research in general:

- **Vodka** is near the bottom of the congener scale, especially well-filtered vodka. In theory it's the gentlest.
- **Clean blanco tequila and gin** sit close to vodka. Gin has botanicals but is usually fairly low in congeners.
- **Aged tequila, rum, and whiskey** carry more wood and fermentation congeners. Bourbon and brandy tend to be at the high end.
- **Mezcal** is a cousin of tequila made from many types of agave, often roasted in earthen pits, and it's usually bottled stronger. It can hit harder for some people, as our [mezcal hangover guide](/never-hungover/mezcal-hangover) explains.

The ranking is useful, but the differences between neighbors are small. The way you drink matters much more than which clear spirit you pick. For a full side-by-side, see our guide to the [least hangover-causing alcohol, ranked](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked).

## The Margarita Problem: Mixers Matter as Much as the Tequila

A lot of tequila hangovers are really margarita hangovers. Here's why a typical bar margarita can be rough:

- **More alcohol than you think.** A standard margarita has tequila plus an orange liqueur such as triple sec. Large and frozen margaritas can easily contain two or three standard drinks in one glass.
- **Sugar makes it easy to drink fast.** Sweet sour mix hides the taste of alcohol, so you finish faster and order another sooner.
- **The tequila in the well is often mixto.** If you don't ask, a bar margarita is commonly made with the cheapest tequila on the rail.

**How to order a gentler tequila drink:**

- **Ask for a 100% agave tequila by name.** Most bars have at least one.
- **Choose a Ranch Water or tequila soda** (tequila, sparkling water, and fresh lime). It's lighter, less sweet, and the bubbles make it more refreshing to sip.
- **Order a Paloma made with fresh grapefruit and soda** rather than a sugary grapefruit soda.
- **If you want a margarita, ask for it with fresh lime and a little agave syrup** (sometimes called a Tommy's-style margarita) and skip the giant sizes.
- **Sip tequila neat or on a large ice cube** if you like the taste. It naturally slows you down.

## How to Drink Tequila Without Wrecking Tomorrow

Even the best bottle needs some help. These habits have the most support:

1. **Count your drinks.** A US standard drink is about 1.5 ounces of 80-proof (40%) spirit. A heavy-handed shot can be more. The number of standard drinks is the biggest single factor in how you'll feel.
2. **Slow down.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink an hour, though this varies a lot. Shots in rapid rounds stack up faster than your liver can keep up.
3. **Eat before and during.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood.
4. **Alternate with water.** A glass of water between drinks slows your pace and helps with the dehydration that alcohol causes by making you pee more.
5. **Avoid mixing lots of different drinks** if it means you lose count. The mixing itself isn't the main issue; the extra total alcohol is. Our article on the [beer before liquor myth](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth) covers this.
6. **Protect your sleep.** Alcohol fragments sleep, which is a big part of why you feel wrecked. Stopping earlier in the evening helps.

Our full guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes through each step with the evidence behind it.

## When a "Tequila Hangover" Is Something More Serious

Most hangovers are miserable but harmless and fade within a day. But some symptoms after a night of drinking aren't a hangover and need real help.

> **When to see a doctor or get emergency care:**
> - **Call 911 (US) right away** if someone is confused, can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has bluish or cold skin, is vomiting while drowsy, or has a seizure. These are signs of alcohol poisoning. Turn them on their side and stay with them until help arrives.
> - **See a doctor the same day** if you're vomiting so much you can't keep water down for many hours, you see blood in your vomit, you have severe stomach pain, or you feel faint when you stand.
> - **Talk to a doctor soon** if your hangovers are getting worse or lasting longer than they used to, you get shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you go without a drink, or you're drinking in the morning to feel normal. Those can be signs your body is reacting to regular alcohol in a way that deserves a check-up.

## Where DHM Fits In

Some people add a supplement to their night out. The most-discussed one is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the brain's response to alcohol. Most of that research is in animals and lab settings, with very limited human data. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in people, and it doesn't change how much alcohol you take in. It's an optional extra, not a replacement for choosing a better tequila and drinking less of it.

If you'd like to try it, people commonly choose [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) as a budget option or [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which adds other ingredients. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands honestly. If you take any medication, check with a pharmacist before adding a supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- **No tequila gives you no hangover.** The amount of alcohol is the main cause.
- **Buy "100% de agave."** It's the most important label check, and it rules out cheap mixtos.
- **Prefer additive-free and blanco** for the cleanest spirit, and check an independent additive-free list, since additives aren't on the label.
- **Watch the mixers.** Sugary, oversized margaritas cause a lot of what people blame on tequila.
- **Drink slowly, eat, alternate with water, and count your drinks.** That does more for tomorrow than any bottle can.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best tequila for no hangover?**

No tequila guarantees no hangover, because the alcohol itself is the main cause. If you want the best odds, choose a bottle labeled "100% de agave" (or "100% agave"), favor a blanco from a producer that is listed as additive-free, and avoid cheap mixto "gold" tequilas made with up to 49% other sugars. Then drink it neat or with soda water and lime, keep the number of drinks modest, eat beforehand, and alternate with water.

**Does 100% agave tequila give you less of a hangover?**

It may, a little, but there is no good evidence from controlled studies that compares 100% agave tequila with mixto tequila directly. The idea is reasonable: 100% agave tequila is made only from blue agave sugars, while mixto can include other sugars and is often sweetened and colored. What the research does show is that the total amount of alcohol you drink matters far more than which bottle it came from.

**Is blanco or reposado tequila better for avoiding a hangover?**

Blanco is usually the safer bet. It is unaged or rested only briefly, so it tends to carry fewer of the wood-derived compounds (congeners) that come from barrel aging. Research on other spirits has linked darker, more congener-rich drinks with somewhat worse hangovers. The difference is modest, though, and a well-made additive-free reposado is a better choice than a sweetened, colored mixto blanco.

**What does additive-free tequila mean?**

Mexican rules allow producers to add small amounts of caramel color, oak extract, glycerin, and sugar-based syrup to tequila without listing them on the label, as long as the total stays under about 1% of the weight. "Additive-free" means the producer uses none of these. Because it isn't printed on bottles, most people check an independent list, such as the Tequila Matchmaker additive-free program, before buying.

**Is tequila better than vodka for a hangover?**

Not reliably. Good vodka is one of the lowest-congener spirits, so in theory it sits at the gentlest end of the scale, and clean blanco tequila is close behind. In practice the difference between the two is small compared with how many drinks you have, how fast you drink them, what you mix them with, and whether you sleep. Choose the one you'll drink slowly and in moderation.

**Why do margaritas give me such a bad hangover?**

Usually because of what's in the glass besides tequila. Bar margaritas are often made with cheap mixto tequila, triple sec (a second alcohol), and sugary sour mix, and they're easy to drink fast. Large or frozen margaritas can hold two or more standard drinks each. A margarita made with 100% agave tequila, fresh lime, and a small amount of agave syrup, sipped slowly, is far gentler.

**Does expensive tequila prevent hangovers?**

No. Price is a weak signal. Some expensive bottles, including many extra añejos and celebrity brands, use additives for sweetness and smoothness, while some modestly priced bottles are 100% agave and additive-free. Read the label for "100% de agave," check the producer on an additive-free list, and remember that even the finest tequila can give you a hangover if you drink too much of it.

**Can DHM help with a tequila hangover?**

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism, mostly in animal and lab research with limited human data. Some people take it with drinks, but there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in humans, and it doesn't change how much alcohol reaches your blood. It's an optional extra on top of drinking less and drinking slower, not a replacement for either.
